summary:
Tilas maps burned peat in Indonesia during the 2026 fire season using NASA's NISAR L-band radar. Fire monitoring in Indonesia mostly counts VIIRS hotspots, which show where a pixel was hot at one moment but not how much land burned, when it burned between overpasses, or which way the fire moved. Smoke also blocks optical satellites for weeks at the peak of the season.
Tilas compares every 12-day NISAR pass over a peat area. Burned forest returns a weaker HV signal, so the pipeline segments the drop into burn scars inside mapped peat units, labels each scar against VIIRS fires, and tracks its area, growth and spread direction pass by pass. Results are split by regency and shown in a web map with a timeline.
In Central Kalimantan, Tilas mapped 82,817 ha of burned peat between 24 July and 28 October 2026, and scar points were 3.5 times more likely than random peat to lie near a VIIRS fire. The output gives restoration teams and local agencies hectares per regency instead of hotspot counts.
details:
What it does

Tilas turns the 2026 peat fire season in Indonesia into mapped hectares. For each study area it shows burn scars on a map, how the burned area grew at every NISAR pass, the direction each fire spread from its first VIIRS detection, and totals per regency. It covers Central Kalimantan, Merauke in South Papua, and Riau.

How it works

1. NISAR L2 GCOV images (HH and HV) are downloaded for every 12-day pass from July to November 2026, mosaicked along the orbit track and averaged to 80 m.

2. HV backscatter comes mostly from leaves and branches, so it drops when the canopy burns. For each pixel on mapped peat (KHG peat units) we keep the largest drop across the season, so scars that regrow or get wet later are still counted.

3. Pixels are grouped into SLIC superpixels and a Multi-Otsu threshold computed from each scene separates burned from unburned. There is no training data and no hand-picked threshold.

4. Each scar is labelled: confirmed (a VIIRS fire within 375 m), hidden (no fire on the scar but a fire within 3 km or heavy smoke from MERRA-2), or verify (forest loss with no fire evidence, often harvest or clearing).

5. For each scar we record the first VIIRS fire date, the first NISAR pass that saw the loss, the spread direction and distance, and the growth rate in hectares per day. Areas are split exactly by regency boundaries.

Results

Central Kalimantan, 24 July to 28 October 2026: 82,817 ha of burned peat in 1,352 scars, 90% with a VIIRS fire within 375 m. The largest increase, 23,886 ha, came between the 4 and 16 October passes. Pulang Pisau had the most burned peat (34,679 ha).

Merauke: 22,012 ha. Riau works as a control: radar found 36,269 ha of forest loss there, but almost none had fire nearby, so Tilas labels it for verification instead of calling it burned.

How we checked it

VIIRS is only used to label scars, never to detect them, so it can serve as an independent check. In Central Kalimantan, 73% of random points inside scars lie within 375 m of a VIIRS fire, against 21% for random peat points (3.5 times more likely). In Merauke the ratio is 2.1. We also tested the idea that smoke hides fires from VIIRS: only 1.6% of the burned area in Central Kalimantan had no fire nearby, so for 2026 we report that the idea is not supported.

Benefits and intended impact

Hotspot counts cannot tell restoration teams, regency disaster agencies or enforcement officers how much peat burned, where, and when. Tilas gives hectares per regency and per peat unit after every NISAR pass, from free NASA data, through smoke and cloud. Rectangular forest loss with no fire nearby is flagged as a lead for possible illegal clearing.

What is creative about it

It uses the new NISAR L-band data, which became public in July 2026, for one of its first fire seasons. It combines radar (what burned) with VIIRS (whether it was fire) without letting one decide for the other, and it tracks each scar over time instead of producing a single before and after map.

Limits

Peat only, so totals are not comparable with national burned-area figures. The 80 m grid misses scars under a few hectares, and surface fires that leave the canopy standing are not detected. NISAR data is still a provisional release, and there is no field validation yet.

Tools

Python (earthaccess, xarray, h5py, rasterio, geopandas, shapely, scikit-image, numpy), Google Colab, MapLibre GL JS for the web app, GitHub Pages for hosting.

Code
